Hi Sara — thanks, great questions and very actionable. TL;DR: the numbers you quoted are achievable with a short Dedicated pilot + SLA exception for TTFT tied to a stated model profile and traffic mix. Below I've sketched the operational differences and next steps.

1) How we define the metrics
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): measured from request arrival at the ingress to the first token emitted by the model (streaming). For non-streaming / batch responses we report time-to-first-byte but most customers treat perceived latency = time until UI shows first token.
- Sustained token/sec: measured as aggregate emitted tokens/sec from the dedicated pool across the window (usually a 1-minute sliding window for SLO calculations).

2) Default Hosted behavior
- Hosted API (multi-tenant): uptime SLA 99.95% (standard), no guaranteed TTFT at the token level for general-purpose streaming — we publish benchmark profiles, and typical p95 TTFT on small-gen sequences is 200–450ms depending on model family and sequence length. Sustained throughput is best-effort and subject to rate limits.

3) Dedicated / Exception path (what we propose for Acme)
- Dedicated pool: committed GPU capacity for predictable throughput. We can offer an SLA that guarantees: 99.9% uptime for the dedicated pool, and a p95 TTFT target for streaming endpoints tied to the agreed model/quantization profile and input size distribution.
- Example commitment (pilot configuration): p95 TTFT <= 400ms for streaming (model: redwood-7B-quant) and aggregate sustained throughput >= 2000 tokens/sec during defined business hours.
- We will tie the SLA to an explicit runbook: model variant, max prompt/response length, concurrency assumptions, and autoscaling/burst policy. Deviations outside these bounds will fall under an exception review rather than a platform breach.

4) Fallbacks and graceful degradation
- If streaming TTFT cannot be met, we can automatically: 1) route to a lower-latency model variant (smaller), or 2) return an early partial token stream and a continuation token to resume generation, or 3) briefly route to sync non-stream path (with consumer-visible tradeoffs). These behaviors are configurable per route.

5) Approval & artifacts
- For formal SLA/exception we need: signed Mutual Action Plan (MAP), a completed SLA Exception Form (we will provide), security questionnaire (youve completed parts already), and target pilot dates. After those, our contracts team issues a short amendment with the TTFT/throughput obligations.

Next steps I propose: I'll attach a draft MAP and the SLA Exception Form; Rishi will add a short technical appendix describing model/profile assumptions. If you confirm the pilot numbers (TTFT p95 <= 400ms, aggregate >= 2k tps), I'll open the formal exception request and loop in contracts.

Connor: can you add the sample autoscale policy and expected GPU footprint for 2k tps (approx)?

Sara — if you're good with this approach I can move to contracts and provide a DocuSign for the MAP + amendment.

Thanks,

Quick technical note on numbers so procurement has the right knobs: 

- TTFT depends heavily on prompt length, KV cache hits, and the model variant. For a quantized 7B model our internal microbenchmarks show p95 TTFT in the 180–350ms range on a cold path for 128-token prompts; longer prompts push that up.
- Sustained tokens/sec is a function of GPU generation and batching. On a dedicated A100-style configuration a single GPU can sustain multiple thousands of tokens/sec (aggregate across batched requests); 2k tokens/sec is a modest dedicated footprint (estimate 3–4 A100s with our batching profile for 250-token average responses at 120 concurrent sessions).
- Autoscale policy we recommend: a hot-queue threshold (queued requests > 250 in 60s -> spin an extra replica) + burst pool with graceful routing to the smaller variant as fallback.

I attached a short appendix for modeling capacity. Happy to run fine-grained capacity sims with your exact prompt distributions.

-Rishi
